edges.description: Inclusion-bearing oligodendrocytes cannot maintain myelin, and connexin 32 is lost from myelin and redistributed into the cytoplasm where it co-localizes with the inclusions.

The oligodendroglial lesion is the primary event and neuronal loss follows it, which is what makes this a primary oligodendrogliopathy rather than a disease in which neurons are the cells that accumulate alpha-synuclein.
On this account the inclusions are assembled from material the oligodendrocyte engulfs, which is how a cell that does not normally express alpha-synuclein comes to hold fibrillar deposits of it.
Impaired myelin maintenance proceeds to axonal degeneration, and the striatonigral and olivopontocerebellar pathways that carry the demyelination are the ones in which the neuronal loss appears.

Impaired autophagic and lysosomal clearance leaves aggregated alpha-synuclein in the cell, so the same pathway whose organelles are found enriched within the inclusions also contributes to their accumulation.
Bioenergetic failure in the affected regions renders the neurons and oligodendrocytes there susceptible to degeneration.
edges.source: Mitochondrial Dysfunction and Coenzyme Q10 Deficiency

edges.description: Microglial activation and T cell infiltration are most abundant in the earliest staged lesions, which is the basis for treating the inflammatory response as a contributor to the neuronal loss rather than only a reaction to it.
Neuronal loss in the nigrostriatal system is the regional pattern that produces the parkinsonian syndrome.
Neuronal loss in the olivopontocerebellar system is the regional pattern that produces the cerebellar syndrome.
Neuronal loss in the brainstem and spinal autonomic nuclei is the regional pattern that produces the autonomic failure.
Denervation of the laryngeal abductor is the focal expression of the same neurogenic process in the motor supply of the vocal folds.
Degeneration of the nigrostriatal system produces the slowness of movement that dominates the parkinsonian presentation.
The same nigrostriatal loss produces parkinsonian rigidity.
Postural instability is one of the parkinsonian features this regional degeneration produces, alongside the bradykinesia and rigidity.
Cerebellar degeneration produces the unsteady wide-based gait of the cerebellar presentation.
Cerebellar involvement contributes the ataxic component of the mixed dysarthria of this disease.

Degeneration of the preganglionic sympathetic neurons removes central sympathetic support for the circulation, so blood pressure falls on standing. Medulla volume is the structure most strongly correlated with the severity of that fall.
Involvement of the pontine micturition centre and of the sacral cord produces the incomplete emptying and retention that distinguish this disease from Parkinson disease.
Vocal folds that cannot abduct narrow the glottis on inspiration, which is heard as stridor.

nodes.description: Glial cytoplasmic inclusions in MSA oligodendrocytes are consistently enriched with lysosomes and peroxisomes, implicating autophagy-lysosomal pathway perturbation in GCI biology. The co-localization of autophagic organelles with alpha-synuclein aggregates suggests that impaired protein clearance mechanisms contribute to GCI formation and accumulation, consistent with broader proteostasis failure in alpha-synucleinopathies.

evidence.reference_title: Distinct ultrastructural phenotypes of glial and neuronal alpha-synuclein inclusions in multiple system atrophy.
evidence.snippet: Oligodendrocytes contained fibrillar GCIs that were consistently enriched with lysosomes and peroxisomes, supporting the involvement of the autophagy pathway in aSyn aggregation in multiple system atrophy.

nodes.description: GCIs may originate through transfer of aggregated alpha-synuclein from neurons to oligodendrocytes via axonal pruning. In this model, alpha-synuclein fibrils first accumulate in neuronal axons as Lewy neurites, and oligodendrocytes then prune and engulf the diseased axonal segments, incorporating the aggregated protein as GCIs. This explains the paradox that mature oligodendrocytes do not normally express alpha-synuclein yet harbor fibrillar inclusions containing the protein.

nodes.description: Degeneration of the autonomic control network in the brainstem and spinal cord. The affected nuclei span the hypothalamus, pontine and medullary autonomic centres, the thoracolumbar intermediolateral column and Onuf's nucleus, and postmortem work places the lesion in the preganglionic autonomic neurons of the brainstem and spinal cord rather than in the periphery. Bladder failure is localized separately from cardiovascular failure, the urinary retention being attributed specifically to pontine and sacral lesions.

nodes.description: MSA is characterized by extensive demyelination in olivopontocerebellar and striatonigral pathways. A distinctive pattern of "distal oligodendrogliopathy-type" demyelination occurs, with early loss of myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG) before myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG). Early and extensive loss of connexin 32 (Cx32) from myelin, and its redistribution into oligodendrocyte cytoplasm co-localizing with GCIs, disrupts inter-glial communication and accelerates myelin breakdown.

nodes.description: Mitochondrial bioenergetic failure, particularly involving the coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) biosynthetic pathway, contributes to MSA pathogenesis. Reduced expression of COQ2 and COQ7 enzymes in disease-affected brain regions correlates with reduced ATP levels. Plasma CoQ10 is significantly lower in MSA patients than controls, independent of COQ2 genotype. This bioenergetic compromise renders vulnerable neurons and oligodendrocytes susceptible to degeneration.

nodes.description: Microglial activation and T-cell infiltration are early and prominent features of MSA pathology. In staged neuropathological lesions, activated microglia/ macrophages and T cells are more abundant in early-stage than late-stage lesions, suggesting neuroinflammation may be an initiating rather than secondary phenomenon. Alpha-synuclein strain characteristics influence the pattern of microglial and astroglial activation.

nodes.description: The pathological hallmark of MSA is the aberrant accumulation of phosphorylated alpha-synuclein in oligodendrocytes, forming glial cytoplasmic inclusions (GCIs), also known as Papp-Lantos bodies. Unlike Parkinson's disease where alpha-synuclein accumulates in neurons, MSA uniquely affects oligodendrocytes. MSA is therefore classified as a primary oligodendrogliopathy with secondary neuronal degeneration. The GCIs disrupt oligodendrocyte function, impair myelin maintenance, and ultimately lead to axonal degeneration.

nodes.description: Neuronal loss in MSA is downstream of the oligodendroglial lesion rather than the primary event, which is what the description of the disease as an oligodendrogliopathy with secondary neuronal degeneration records. Demyelination, bioenergetic failure and an early inflammatory response converge on the neurons of the striatonigral, olivopontocerebellar and central autonomic systems, and which of those systems is worst affected is what decides whether a patient presents with parkinsonism or with cerebellar ataxia.

nodes.description: Neuronal loss, gliosis and glial cytoplasmic inclusions in the putamen, with deterioration of the nigrostriatal system more broadly. This is the regional pattern behind the parkinsonian presentation and the reason MSA-P was formerly called striatonigral degeneration.
